restored.judge: (b) tail 'belongs in a sourced class report' is meta about the student's report, not about nature/authorities
restored.skeptic: Main clause is an institutional fact a student learns from: DOH situation reports list medical teams and clean-water advice for typhoon-hit areas, i.e. how a national authority delivers health support. The tail 'belongs in a sourced class report' is only a light appositive wrapper, not the point of the sentence; the fact stands alone as a feed card.

restored.judge: (b) framed as source-hierarchy talk ('remain a secondary source') rather than a fact about hazards or support
restored.skeptic: Institutional fact, not source-hierarchy talk: Project NOAH is a DOST hazard-mapping project whose maps identify flood-prone places used for typhoon support planning. 'Remain a secondary source' is mild attribution around a real, accurate fact (NOAH began under DOST, later moved to UP, so 'older DOST project' is correct). Same class as 'PAGASA bulletins are official typhoon warnings'.

restored.judge: (a) main clause is advice to gather both language versions; the bilingual-warning fact is subordinate
restored.skeptic: The stand-alone fact is that official warnings are issued in both Filipino and English so authorities reach more households; that is directly about how authorities support communities. The second clause is descriptive ('can show how authorities try to reach more households'), not an imperative gathering instruction, and it carries the 'why' of the fact.

restored.judge: (b) meta about what counts as 'support information' for the task rather than a fact about recovery
restored.skeptic: Read alone, a student learns a real institutional fact: NDRRMC post-disaster reports count houses repaired and families served, and government support continues into recovery rather than ending when the wind dies. The 'are still support information' phrasing is a light framing wrapper, not competency/task meta; the content is exactly what the competency covers.

restored.judge: (b) second clause is meta advice about which pages are 'the right source', not about nature
restored.skeptic: The load-bearing clause is a stand-alone consensus science fact: the Moon's gravity, with the Sun's, causes the tidal rise and fall. The tail ('secondary physics pages are the right source') is a mild pointer, not the substance; a grade-8 student reading the card alone still learns the correct cause of tides. Real fact wrapped in mild attribution = keep.

restored.judge: (b) 'Modern source papers discuss...' — sentence is about papers, not a stand-alone fact
restored.skeptic: Underneath 'papers discuss' is a real engineering fact: fish passages and slower-turning turbines are mitigation measures that let tidal plants reduce harm to migrating animals. Same pattern as the KEEP example 'textbooks cite lactase persistence...'; the attribution is light and the fact is verifiable and grade-appropriate.

restored.judge: (b) main clause is 'sources discuss whether...' — meta talk about sources
restored.skeptic: Contains two genuine facts: tides arrive later each day (about 50 min/day), so tidal generation windows drift relative to evening peak demand, which is a real siting consideration separate from the size of the range. The 'sources discuss' wrapper is mild attribution around correct physics and grid-planning content a student learns from.

restored.judge: (b) 'Papers on tidal-stream farms discuss...' — subject is the papers, not the wake effect
restored.skeptic: The content is a real fluid-dynamics fact: in a tidal-stream array, each turbine leaves a slowed wake, so turbines must be spaced so one does not rob the next of current. 'Papers on ... discuss' is only light attribution; the wake-interaction fact stands alone and is correct.

restored.judge: (b) META: trailing clause is about what 'secondary biology pages use ... without naming a scare list' — writer/source talk, not nature
restored.skeptic: Main clause is a stand-alone, correct science fact a grade-9 student learns from: harmful mutations change a protein's shape so a cell process fails. The trailing 'secondary biology pages use... as the usual disease example' is light attribution of the same kind the judge kept in rows 015 ('sources treat many knock-out changes as damaging'), 024 ('sources mention this') and 026 ('sources warn'); 'without naming a scare list' is harmless. A real fact wrapped in mild attribution is a keep; drop would be inconsistent with the kept siblings.

restored.judge: (b) META: 'secondary sources refuse a single label without naming the trait' is about sources, not the mutation
restored.skeptic: The sentence's content is a consensus science fact: a gain-of-function mutation can be beneficial, harmful, or both depending on the trait/context. The 'so secondary sources refuse a single label' clause is attribution wrapping that fact, not a sentence about sources instead of nature (compare kept row 007 'a beneficial example sources discuss' and row 038 'a wording secondary biology sources keep careful'). Read alone a student learns the correct lesson that effect depends on the trait; keep.

restored.judge: (a) second half is advice on how to present the gathered 'ways' as a pair; card reads as task instruction
restored.skeptic: The main clause is a real, consensus safety fact a G10 student learns from: airbags are supplementary restraints designed to work with a fastened seatbelt (an unbelted occupant can be hurt by the bag). 'Crash-test sources warn' is light attribution. The tail ('present them as a pair, not as rivals') is a takeaway that still holds read alone (belt + airbag together, not either/or); it is a mild advice wrapper on a genuine fact, unlike F-7-001/018/019 where no fact is stated at all. A real fact with mild attribution/advice tail is a keep.

restored.judge: (a) advice on presenting information (save a map and attach it to a report) built around an app UI detail (a FaultFinder print button) that is not a science fact and is unverifiable; teaches nothing about faults
restored.skeptic: card_form is 'method' and G7-E-4 is the competency that is literally about using the PHIVOLCS FaultFinder to locate the nearest active fault to a place. Read alone, the sentence tells a student a real, verifiable tool capability (the FaultFinder web app has a print/save function that outputs a map showing a chosen location, e.g. the school, and the nearest active fault) — a genuine procedure step in the same class as kept rows like 'label the sample with date and place' or 'plot coils on the x-axis'. The 'attach to a report' clause is only the tail, not the substance; the load-bearing content is that FaultFinder produces a school-to-nearest-fault map you can save. Not a factual error and not meta talk about sources.
